addedResources.name: AlgoMaster System Design practice - clock, gossip and lease drills
addedResources.use: Use only the named problems: Advance a Lamport Logical Clock, Compare Two Vector Clocks, Update a Vector Clock on Receive, Advance a Hybrid Logical Clock, Simulate Gossip Rumor Spread and Implement a Lease Lock with Fencing Tokens. Each states its function signature and checks small deterministic cases.

units.title: Wall and monotonic clocks, drift, skew, backward jumps and synchronization uncertainty
outcomes: Explain when to use a wall clock and when to use a monotonic clock, and why monotonic readings cannot be compared across nodes.
Derive drift accumulation from a parts-per-million rate and state skew, backward jumps and NTP error sources for a given setup.
Treat a clock reading as an interval with stated uncertainty and say what ordering it cannot support.
units.why: Ordering by wall timestamps is the most common silent-loss bug in this section. Clocks look simple until a step, a pause or a skew window reorders two writes.

next.note: Replace wall timestamps with a causal order where wall time cannot be trusted.
See what a lease must assume about these same clocks and pauses.

study.title: Unreliable clocks
study.locator: Chapter 9, Unreliable Clocks (p. 358), Monotonic Versus Time-of-Day Clocks (pp. 359-360), Clock Synchronization and Accuracy (pp. 360-361), Relying on Synchronized Clocks with Figure 9-3 (pp. 362-364), Clock readings with a confidence interval (pp. 364-365)

study.title: Clock synchronisation and monotonic clocks
study.locator: Section 3.2, Slides 52 to 59: NTP request and response stamps, skew estimate, slew and step thresholds, Java currentTimeMillis versus nanoTime example; Exercise 7

study.title: Why wall-clock time fails
study.locator: Theory, Why wall-clock time fails: quartz drift, NTP skew range, leap-second cases and VM pauses; Warnings on ORDER BY created_at and leap-second timing code
study.depth: Use as review after DDIA and the notes. Treat its cloud skew ranges and TrueTime bounds as reported figures from its cited sources, not targets you must reproduce.

focus: A time-of-day clock reads wall time and can step backward. A monotonic clock measures elapsed time on one node and its absolute value is meaningless elsewhere.
Drift is a rate error in one clock. Skew is the difference between two clocks at one instant. NTP estimates skew under a symmetric-delay assumption that queueing can break.

NTP slews below 125 ms by varying the rate up to 500 ppm, steps between 125 ms and 1,000 s by resetting the clock, and panics at or above 1,000 s, leaving the fix to an operator. A step is a backward jump for wall readers.
A reading is an interval, not a point. DDIA builds this from drift since last sync plus server uncertainty plus round-trip time.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the book's drift example: at 200 ppm a clock resynced every 30 seconds drifts \(200 \times 10^{-6} \times 30 = 0.006\) seconds, or 6 ms, and resynced once a day drifts \(200 \times 10^{-6} \times 86{,}400 = 17.28\) seconds, which the book rounds to 17 seconds. State which resync interval each number assumes.
traps: Comparing monotonic readings from two nodes. They start from unrelated boot points, so the comparison is meaningless even when each node is correct.
Using a wall clock for elapsed time. A step or leap second can make the difference negative or inflated; use a monotonic source for intervals.
Reading NTP as a bound. NTP gives a best-effort estimate with no stated confidence interval, so design the consumer to tolerate the full skew window.

selfTest.q: Why can two writes 3 ms apart get timestamps in the wrong order even with good NTP?
selfTest.a: Skew between the writers can exceed the real gap. DDIA Figure 9-3 shows writes at 42.004 and 42.003 seconds where the causally later write carries the smaller stamp, so last-write-wins drops the increment.

selfTest.q: What is the difference between drift and skew?
selfTest.a: Drift is one clock running fast or slow over time. Skew is the difference between two clocks read at the same instant.

selfTest.q: When does NTP slew, step or refuse?
selfTest.a: Slew below 125 ms by adjusting the rate, step between 125 ms and 1,000 s by resetting the clock, and panic at or above 1,000 s, leaving the fix to an operator.

selfTest.q: Why is a clock reading better described as an interval?
selfTest.a: Quartz drift since last sync, server uncertainty and network delay each add error. The true time lies somewhere in the resulting range, and digits below that width carry no meaning.

practice.name: Building Distributed Systems Timekeeper PH-1: Read System Clock and Detect Backward Jumps
practice.locator: Task PH-1: sample the system clock in a loop and record backward jumps
practice.note: Keep the jump log. It is the evidence you cite when you claim wall time moved backward on your machine.

practice.name: Building Distributed Systems Timekeeper PH-2: Implement Monotonic Clock Wrapper
practice.locator: Task PH-2: wrap the system clock so the result never decreases and state what is lost
practice.note: State the loss in your own words: the wrapper hides the step but keeps no wall meaning, so it cannot order events across nodes.

fit.note: DDIA plus the notes derivation workbook cover all three topics at explain and measure depth, and the two free Timekeeper drills give checked practice.

units.title: Happens-before, Lamport clocks and total-order tie breaking
outcomes: Define happens-before from its three rules and decide for event pairs whether one precedes the other or they are concurrent.
Compute Lamport timestamps for a small message history with rules IR1 and IR2, and state which orders the stamps prove and which they leave open.
Build the total order with node-id tie breaking and explain why it is causal yet arbitrary on concurrent events.
units.why: Causal order is what a system can know without synchronized clocks. Lamport stamps are the cheapest way to label it, and their limits motivate every later clock in this section.

next.note: Detect the concurrency that Lamport stamps hide.
Keep causality while staying close to wall time.

study.title: Partial order, logical clocks and the total order
study.locator: The Partial Ordering (happens-before rules 1 to 3), Logical Clocks (Clock Condition, C1, C2, IR1, IR2) and Ordering the Events Totally with the five-rule mutual-exclusion algorithm
study.depth: Skim Anomalous Behavior and Physical Clocks on first pass. They motivate bounded physical clocks, which return in the hybrid clock unit.

study.title: Happens-before and Lamport clocks workbook
study.locator: Section 3.3, Slides 60 to 64: message reorder example, physical timestamps against causality, happens-before and concurrency; Section 4.1, Slides 65 to 68: Lamport algorithm, properties and total order; Exercises 8, 10 and 11

focus: Happens-before has three rules: same-node order, send before matching receive, and transitivity. Concurrent means no message path either way, not simultaneity.

IR1 increments the clock between successive events. IR2 attaches the send stamp to the message, and the receiver moves past \(\max(\text{local}, t)\) and adds one, so the receive itself counts as an event.
The Clock Condition says \(a \rightarrow b\) implies \(C(a) < C(b)\). The converse is false, and equal stamps do not imply concurrency: the notes show two different events that both stamp 3.
The pair \((L, N)\) ordered lexicographically is a causal linear extension of happens-before. Concurrent pairs fall wherever the node names put them.
The algorithm assumes a crash-stop model. Crash recovery needs the stamp in stable storage, or a restarted node reuses low stamps.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write IR1 and IR2, then stamp this history: A has a local event, A sends m to B, B receives m, B has a local event, and C has one local event throughout. Result: A stamps 1 and 2, B stamps 3 and 4, C stamps 1. State that B stamps 3 and 4 prove nothing about C, since C is concurrent with all four.
traps: Reading \(L(a) < L(b)\) as proof that a caused b. It only rules out b happening before a; a and b may be concurrent.
Skipping the plus one on receive. Then successive receives of same-stamped messages stop advancing the clock and C1 breaks.
Assuming the paper's mutual-exclusion algorithm works over a real network. It assumes every message is eventually received in order, so a real build must add sequence numbers and retransmission.

selfTest.q: A sends m then has a local event; B receives m. Which pairs are ordered and which are concurrent?
selfTest.a: Send precedes receive and each node's own events are ordered. B's receive is concurrent with A's later local event, since no message connects them.

selfTest.q: Stamps read \(L(a) = 2\) and \(L(b) = 5\). Could a have caused b?
selfTest.a: Possibly, but not proven. The stamps rule out b happening before a and leave happened-before versus concurrent open.

selfTest.q: Two events share stamp 3. Are they the same event, ordered, or concurrent?
selfTest.a: Nothing follows from the stamp alone. They may be ordered or concurrent; identity needs the (timestamp, node) pair.

selfTest.q: Why does the total order need node names, and what does it settle for concurrent events?
selfTest.a: Names make every pair comparable so each event has one place in line. For concurrent events the order is deterministic but arbitrary, while happened-before pairs always keep their order.

units.title: Vector clock comparison, concurrency and dotted version vectors
outcomes: Compare two vector timestamps and return before, after, equal or concurrent, with the causal-history reading of the result.
Run the vector update rules on a message history and explain what entry \(T[i]\) records about node \(N_i\).
State what dotted version vectors change for per-key concurrent writes and when to reach for them.
units.why: Lamport stamps hide concurrency. Vectors expose it, which is what conflict detection and repair need in later sections.

next.note: Compress the vector to constant space with a physical clock.
Use vectors for multi-key conflict detection and deletes.

study.title: Vector clocks workbook
study.locator: Section 4.1, Slides 69 to 72: vector algorithm, the worked example where C learns A's two events through B, and the comparison rules; Exercises 12 and 13
study.depth: Exercise 13 names three event pairs, send(m2) with send(m3), send(m3) with send(m5) and send(m5) with send(m9). Answer each pair from both the Lamport and the vector columns.

study.title: Dotted version vectors
study.locator: Theory, Dotted version vectors: server-keyed vectors, one dot per value, and the rule for when clients outnumber servers
study.depth: Use as review after the notes. The Riak sibling-explosion story is a reported deployment result, not a setup you reproduce here.

focus: On an event at node \(N_i\), increment \(T[i]\). On send, attach \(T\). On receive, take the element-wise maximum, then increment \(T[i]\). Entry \(T[i]\) counts events of \(N_i\) observed so far.
A vector stamps a causal history: event plus everything before it. So \(V(a) < V(b)\) holds exactly when \(a \rightarrow b\), equality means the same event, and incomparability means concurrency.
The worked example shows indirect knowledge: when C receives from B, its A entry jumps to 2 without ever hearing from A, because B already knew.

Dotted version vectors key the vector on servers, not clients, and tag each value with one dot. A put subsumes the siblings its context observed, so only truly concurrent siblings survive, which ends the client-id explosion.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compare \([2, 2, 0]\) with \([0, 0, 1]\): the first leads in entries 0 and 1, the second in entry 2, so they are concurrent. Then run a receive at process 0 with local \([1, 0, 0]\) and message \([0, 1, 0]\): the merge is \([1, 1, 0]\), plus one for the receive, giving \([2, 1, 0]\).
traps: Treating a smaller vector as an earlier event in wall time. The order is causal inclusion, not time, and concurrent vectors are unordered by definition.
Merging without the final increment. The receive is a new event at the receiver, and skipping it undercounts the receiver's own entry.
Reusing vectors across a membership change. Entries are positional per member, so a join or replacement needs a new epoch or a map keyed by member id, not a silent index shift.

selfTest.q: Vectors read \([1, 2, 0]\) and \([1, 3, 0]\). What is their relation, and what does it mean?
selfTest.a: Before: every entry of the first is at most the second's, with entry 1 smaller. The first event happened before the second.

selfTest.q: Why does C's A entry become 2 after receiving B's vector, with no message from A?
selfTest.a: B's vector already recorded two A events, and the element-wise maximum copies that knowledge. Vectors carry transitive history, not just direct contact.

selfTest.q: Two replicas hold dots \((s_1, 5)\) and \((s_2, 3)\) for one key with incomparable contexts. Siblings or overwrite?
selfTest.a: Siblings. Neither context subsumes the other, so the writes are concurrent and both values stay until something resolves them.

selfTest.q: What breaks if you compare vectors stamped under different member sets?
selfTest.a: Positions no longer name the same members, so before, after and concurrent verdicts are meaningless. Re-key or re-epoch on membership change.

practice.name: Compare Two Vector Clocks
practice.locator: Implement `compare`: `before` when every entry of `a` is at most `b`'s with one smaller, `after` for the reverse, `equal` for identical, else `concurrent`
practice.note: Write the four-way rule from memory first. The checker tests the boundary between before and concurrent.

units.title: Hybrid logical clock state, persistence and implementation
outcomes: Run the Figure 5 send and receive rules on a short trace and explain what each of \(l\) and \(c\) records.
State the proved bounds on \(l - pt\) and on \(c\) with the synchronization assumption each one needs.
Persist HLC state across restarts and bound NTP steps with the reset and ignore-out-of-bounds rules.
units.why: Vectors cost a slot per node. HLC keeps causality in constant space while staying near wall time, which is what database timestamps use in practice.

next.note: Stamp unique IDs with a clock that is causal and wall-readable.
See where even a bounded clock still needs fencing.

study.title: HLC algorithm, bounds and resilience
study.locator: Section 3.3 with Figure 5 (send, local and receive rules), Theorems 1 to 4 with Corollaries 1 to 4, Section 3.4 (superposition on NTP), Section 4.1 (reset and ignore rules) and Section 5.1 (AWS c-value table)
study.depth: Read the paper as version TR 2014-04. Work the naive-algorithm counterexample in Section 3.2 before Figure 5, so the missing plus one reads as the fix.

study.title: HLC summary and deployment numbers
study.locator: Theory, Hybrid Logical Clocks: state pair, 64-bit packing and the CockroachDB, YugabyteDB and MongoDB users
study.depth: Use as review after the paper. Its one-line receive rule glosses the four cases of Figure 5, so trust the paper for implementation.

focus: State is \((l_j, c_j)\). On a local event or send, \(l_j\) becomes \(\max(l_j, pt_j)\); \(c_j\) increments if \(l_j\) is unchanged and resets otherwise. On receive, \(l_j\) becomes \(\max(l_j, l_m, pt_j)\), and \(c_j\) follows the four-way rule for which of the three inputs won.
Comparison is lexicographic. Theorem 1 gives causality one way: happened-before implies a smaller stamp, never the reverse, exactly like Lamport.

Theorem 2 keeps \(l\) at or ahead of \(pt\), and Corollary 1 bounds \(|l - pt|\) by the synchronization uncertainty \(\epsilon\). Theorem 4 reads \(c\) as the length of a same-\(l\) causal chain, which Corollary 3 bounds further.

HLC only reads the physical clock and never writes it, so NTP clients are unaffected. On a bound violation the node resets \(l\) to \(pt\) with \(c = 0\), ignores out-of-bounds messages, and raises an alert.
In the paper's AWS run, \(c\) stays near zero: about 84 percent of events carry \(c = 0\) on four nodes. That is their setup with a stratum-2 server, not a number you must reproduce.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run Figure 5 from \((0, 0)\): local event at \(pt = 10\) gives \((10, 0)\), another local at \(pt = 10\) gives \((10, 1)\), a receive at \(pt = 10\) of remote \((12, 4)\) gives \((12, 5)\), and a local at \(pt = 50\) gives \((50, 0)\). Name which case of the receive rule fires each time.
traps: Reading \((l, c)\) as wall time. \(l\) can run ahead of \(pt\) by up to \(\epsilon\), so only differences above that width carry causal meaning.
Restarting with \(l = 0\). Pre-crash stamps stay in other nodes' state, so a fresh zero rewinds this node's stamps. Persist the maximum \(l\) to stable storage and reload it.
Packing the pair into 64 bits and comparing the packed integer across layouts. Decode to \((l, c)\) first, since layouts disagree on the split.

selfTest.q: A local event sees \(pt = 5\) with state \((7, 0)\). What is the new stamp, and why does it not follow the wall clock down?
selfTest.a: \((7, 1)\). The maximum keeps 7, and the counter records the event at that level, so stamps stay monotonic across the backward step.

selfTest.q: What do Theorems 2 and 3 together say about a stamp with \(l\) far ahead of \(pt\)?
selfTest.a: Some causally prior event saw a physical clock equal to that \(l\). A large gap means the node learned a fast remote clock, not that its own clock is wrong.

selfTest.q: Why does the paper bound \(c\) by chain length rather than by node count in practice?
selfTest.a: Theorem 4 ties each count to a distinct same-\(l\) causal predecessor. Long same-millisecond chains are rare, so measured \(c\) stays in single digits while the node-count bound is loose.

selfTest.q: An NTP step pushes \(pt\) an hour forward. What fires, and what is lost?
selfTest.a: The masking bound breaks, so the node resets \(l\) to \(pt\) with \(c = 0\) and ignores far-ahead messages with an alert. Causality survives; closeness to true time waits on NTP.

practice.name: Advance a Hybrid Logical Clock
practice.locator: Implement `local` and `receive` per the four-way rule, including unchanged and backward `physicalTime`; the second example resets the counter when physical time strictly wins
practice.note: The page's rule matches Figure 5. Add persistence of the pair and the reset-and-ignore policy around it in your own harness.

units.title: Unique identifiers, incarnation numbers and restart-safe identity
outcomes: Choose an ID scheme, random, wall-clock-ordered or Lamport pair, and state its collision, ordering and coordination costs.
Assign incarnation numbers so a restarted process never reuses a live identity, and say who may increment them.
Persist the identity state that makes restart safe, and test the dual-incarnation case.
units.why: Every dedup key, fencing check and membership entry names an actor. A reused identity turns an ordinary restart into a split brain.

next.note: Carry incarnations into versioned membership views.
Use incarnations plus tokens to fence stale holders.

study.title: ID generators and Lamport pairs
study.locator: Chapter 10, ID Generators and Logical Clocks: autoincrement and linearizable single-node IDs, random UUIDs and wall-clock timestamp schemes (pp. 417-419); Lamport (counter, node ID) pairs with the Aaliyah, Bryce and Caleb ordering (pp. 420-422)

study.title: Incarnation numbers against false suspicion
study.locator: Section 4.2, Suspicion mechanism: incarnation initialized at join, incremented only by the suspected node itself, Alive with a higher number refuting Suspect and Failed

study.title: Unique IDs under partition
study.locator: Challenge 2: `generate` with any ID type, tested with `--node-count 3 --availability total --nemesis partition`; uniqueness is checked, ordering and monotonicity are not

focus: Single-node autoincrement is linearizable: a completed post always gets the smaller ID. No distributed scheme in this unit keeps that without coordination.
Random 128-bit IDs need no communication and give no order. Wall-clock schemes sort roughly but lean on NTP, a shard or random part, and a per-shard sequence for same-millisecond uniqueness.
A Lamport pair is unique when node IDs are unique, and orders causally but not by wall time. Two nodes that never communicate can hold wildly different counters.
SWIM incarnations start at join and only the named node increments its own, when it sees itself suspected. A higher number overrides older Suspect and Failed reports about that member.
Restart safety is persisted state: an epoch or the maximum counter on stable storage, reloaded before the first new ID. Without it the counter restarts at zero and old and new IDs collide.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, show the restart hole: node B issues (counter 1..50, node B), crashes without persisting, restarts at counter 0 and reissues counter 1, colliding with a live record. Then fix it: persist an epoch that increments once per restart, so post-restart IDs read (epoch 2, counter 1) and never equal epoch 1 IDs.
traps: Reading wall-clock ID order as causal order. A fast clock stamps an earlier write above a later one from a slow clock, and one NTP step reorders a single node's IDs.
Letting another node bump a member's incarnation. Only the member itself increments; anything else lets a partitioner forge a refutation.
Rejoining with the same identity and a reset counter. The group still holds the old incarnation, so rejoin as a new epoch or a new member, never as a silent reset.

selfTest.q: A billion random version-4 IDs are generated. About how likely is one collision?
selfTest.a: About \(10^{-19}\). With 122 random bits the birthday term is near \(10^{18}/2^{123}\), vanishingly small but not zero, and it says nothing about order.

selfTest.q: Two Snowflake IDs sort correctly. Does the earlier-sorting record causally precede the other?
selfTest.a: Not proven. Sort order follows wall clocks plus shard and sequence parts; skew or a step can invert it relative to causality.

selfTest.q: Node X is suspected at incarnation 3, then broadcasts Alive at incarnation 4. A late Suspect for incarnation 3 arrives after. What does the group keep?
selfTest.a: Alive at 4. The higher incarnation wins, and the stale report for 3 is dropped.

selfTest.q: Why must the epoch live on stable storage rather than in memory?
selfTest.a: Memory resets on crash, which replays epoch 1. Stable storage survives, so the next boot provably moves to epoch 2.

units.title: Heartbeats, observation windows, detector completeness and accuracy, and suspicion thresholds
outcomes: Explain what a heartbeat proves and what silence cannot prove, using the observation-window idea.
State detector completeness against accuracy, and say which side a shorter timeout buys.
Compare fixed thresholds with adaptive ones, and name the workload change that breaks each.
units.why: Every membership and failover decision starts as a suspicion. This vocabulary decides whether a pause looks like death, before any threshold is tuned.

next.note: Replace the fixed timeout with a tunable suspicion signal.
Spread suspicions without a central watcher.

study.title: Fault detection and timeouts
study.locator: Chapter 9, Fault Detection (p. 351): explicit crash signals versus timeout guessing; Timeouts and Unbounded Delays (pp. 352-353): the false-positive against detection-delay balance, the 2d+r bound and congestion causes

study.title: Direct and indirect probing
study.locator: Section 3.1, SWIM failure detector: one random ping per protocol period, k indirect ping-reqs when the ack misses, and the end-of-period check

study.title: Heartbeat and timeout sizing
study.locator: Theory, Heartbeats and timeouts: p99 plus jitter sizing with a 2x to 4x margin, and the reported etcd, Kubernetes, TCP keepalive and Redis Cluster numbers
study.depth: Use as review after DDIA and SWIM. Its deployment numbers are reported figures from their sources, not values to copy into your detector.

study.title: Election timeouts affect progress, majority affects safety
study.locator: MIT 6.5840 Spring 2026 Lecture 6 notes: when a peer starts an election, the at-most-one-leader vote rules, and how to choose the election timeout
study.depth: Read for the timing lens only: needless elections are slow but safe, and an old leader may still think it leads. Do not start the Raft lab.

focus: A received heartbeat proves the sender was alive at send time, nothing more. Silence inside one window proves nothing: delay, pause, overload and death look identical until the window closes.

Completeness means every crash is eventually suspected; accuracy means no live node is. A shorter timeout buys completeness and spends accuracy, and DDIA shows premature suspicion can cascade under load.
Explicit signals beat guessing where they exist: a refused connection or a crash notification, as HBase sends, reports death without waiting out a timeout.
SWIM separates the two failure modes: a direct miss may be a bad path, so k indirect probes ask whether anyone can reach the target before suspicion.
Raft shows the split this section keeps: timeouts and heartbeats drive progress (elections, suppression), while majority votes carry safety when the old leader is still talking.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, derive the 2d+r bound: with at most d delay each way and at most r handling time, every successful request answers within 2d+r, so later silence proves something failed. Then name the two bounds a real deployment lacks, which is why the timeout becomes a tradeoff instead of a proof.
traps: Treating a missed heartbeat as death. The detector output is suspicion with a threshold, and acting on it needs fencing or a quorum, as later units show.
Tuning the timeout down to detect faster without costing anything. Faster detection spends accuracy, and false convictions add failover load exactly when the system is slowest.
Copying a vendor timeout into a different network. A 10x ratio that fits one RTT and jitter budget misfires under another; size from your own p99 plus margin.

selfTest.q: A node misses two heartbeat windows, then answers. Was it dead during the silence?
selfTest.a: Unknowable from heartbeats alone. Delay, pause, overload or a short crash with recovery all fit; the detector can only report suspicion, not the cause.

selfTest.q: What do completeness and accuracy each promise, and which one breaks first when load spikes?
selfTest.a: Completeness promises crashed nodes are eventually suspected; accuracy promises live ones are not. Load spikes break accuracy first, through false suspicion.

selfTest.q: Why does SWIM probe indirectly before suspecting, instead of suspecting on the first missed ack?
selfTest.a: A direct miss may be a faulty path rather than a faulty target. If any of k others reaches the target, the initiator learns liveness without a false report.

selfTest.q: Raft holds an unnecessary election. What breaks: safety or progress?
selfTest.a: Progress only, for a while. Majority voting still permits at most one leader per term, so the cost is delay, which the notes call slow but safe.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a configurable heartbeat detector in the deterministic network simulation, with suspicion traces under delay, pause and partition schedules.
units.stopWhen: You derive 2d+r with its two missing bounds from memory, and can call each of delay, pause, overload and death from the same silence trace.

fit.note: DDIA plus SWIM cover vocabulary and mechanism at explain and derive depth, with detector practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: False suspicion, a phi-accrual detector and detection-delay measurement
outcomes: Name the non-death causes of silence, pause, overload and loss bursts, and show one on a heartbeat trace.
Implement the phi computation over a sliding window and trigger suspicion at a chosen threshold.
Measure detection delay against false-suspicion rate across thresholds and window sizes on one trace.
units.why: One fixed timeout forces one tradeoff on every consumer. Phi separates the suspicion signal from the decision, so each consumer picks its own point on the curve.

next.note: Feed the suspicion signal into gossip spread.
See what a pause costs when authority has an expiry.

study.title: The phi accrual detector
study.locator: Section III (accrual abstraction with per-application thresholds), Section IV-A with Equation 2 (meaning of phi), Section IV-B with Equations 3 and 4 and Figure 4 (window sampling with the normal estimate), Section V-A (Japan to Switzerland UDP setup) and Experiments 1 to 3 with Figures 8 and 9
study.depth: Read the paper as report IS-RR-2004-010. Its normal approximation misleads under bursty delay, so rerun the measurement on a pause trace too, as the last focus point says.

study.title: Phi in production
study.locator: Theory, Phi-accrual detectors with the Cassandra example: window of 1,000 arrivals, threshold 8 with the 0.434 factor, and the pause guard
study.depth: Treat the threshold-8 silence seconds as that deployment's arithmetic on its own gossip interval, not a portable constant.

study.title: Suspicion before conviction
study.locator: Section 4.2: the suspicion timeout trades longer detection time for fewer false detections
study.depth: Read for the tradeoff sentence only; the full mechanism returns in the gossip and membership units.

focus: Phi is \(\phi(t) = -\log_{10} P_{later}(t)\), where \(P_{later}\) comes from a normal model fitted to the sliding window of past inter-arrival times. Each extra unit divides the modeled late probability by ten.
The window keeps arrival times with running sum and sum of squares, giving \(\mu\) and \(\sigma^2\). The threshold is per application: low means fast with mistakes, high means slow with few.

On the paper's intercontinental trace, most late beats are caught by threshold 2, while detection time climbs sharply past thresholds 10 to 11. Both numbers belong to 100 ms heartbeats over that link, not to your network.

Bursts break the model: the trace holds a 1,093-message loss burst of about two minutes. A normal fit on calm samples calls that death with high phi, which is why deployments add pause guards and minimum-deviation floors.
Detection time splits into propagation plus the threshold's equivalent timeout. Raising the threshold only spends the second term, never the first.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, compute phi for a heartbeat 120 ms late when the window says \(\mu = 100\) ms and \(\sigma = 5\) ms: the deviation is 4 sigma, so \(1 - F\) is about \(3.2 \times 10^{-5}\) and phi is about 4.5. State the normal-model assumption the 4.5 depends on.
traps: Reading phi as the probability the node is dead. It is the modeled rarity of this much lateness; death needs a threshold policy plus fencing or a quorum.
Moving a threshold across networks. Threshold 8 means different silence seconds under 100 ms and 1 s heartbeats, so recalibrate the curve per deployment.
Sizing the window in samples while jitter changes the rate. Under bursty loss the window fills with gap samples and the mean drifts; test with pause traces, not only steady ones.

selfTest.q: Two applications watch one phi signal with thresholds 2 and 8. A beat arrives very late. Who suspects, and who may act?
selfTest.a: Both see the same phi curve, but 2 trips earlier and risks a false call while 8 waits. Each acts only under its own policy; the signal itself decides nothing.

selfTest.q: Why does the paper replay recorded traces instead of testing detectors live side by side?
selfTest.a: Replay feeds every detector the identical arrival sequence, so threshold and window differences, not network luck, explain the mistake and delay curves.

selfTest.q: A two-minute loss burst arrives during calm operation. What does phi report, and what should the deployment do?
selfTest.a: Phi climbs steeply and crosses most thresholds: a false suspicion under the model. A pause guard or deviation floor should absorb it before any failover acts.

selfTest.q: Threshold rises from 2 to 12. Which part of detection time grows, and which never shrinks?
selfTest.a: The equivalent timeout from the threshold grows. Propagation delay stays, so detection never beats the round trip no matter the threshold.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: a phi-accrual detector over recorded heartbeat traces with pause and burst schedules, reporting detection-delay against false-suspicion curves per threshold with seeds retained.
units.stopWhen: You compute the reproduce phi from memory with its assumption stated, and can place any threshold choice on the delay-versus-mistakes curve for your own trace.

fit.note: Paper plus handbook cover the detector and its tuning at implement and measure depth, with trace practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: Gossip dissemination, a gossip membership implementation and convergence measurement
outcomes: Derive per-round growth and rounds-to-cover for a fanout and size, and state the no-duplicate-contact assumption.
Implement push gossip over a peer list that converges with partitions and heals after them.
Measure messages per operation and convergence time from a Maelstrom run and compare against the rumor model.
units.why: Gossip trades immediate agreement for eventual convergence at constant per-node cost. It carries membership, and later repair, without any coordinator.

next.note: Run join, leave and replacement over this dissemination.
Compare rumor spread with digest-based repair.

study.title: Infection-style dissemination
study.locator: Section 4.1: piggybacking on ping, ping-req and ack with no extra packets, the bounded buffer, and preferring updates gossiped fewer times

study.title: Broadcast challenges 3a to 3c
study.locator: Challenge 3a (single node), 3b (five nodes, no partitions) and 3c (five nodes with `--nemesis partition`); the checker tests convergence of every value to every node, not order or recency
study.depth: Stop at 3c. The 3d and 3e efficiency thresholds belong to their own 25-node setup and are not targets here.

focus: Each round multiplies the informed set: \(I_{r+1} = \min(n, I_r \times (1 + f))\) for fanout \(f\), assuming every contact reaches a new node. Real contacts repeat, so the model is an upper bound on speed.

SWIM sends no dedicated gossip packets: membership updates ride the failure-detector traffic. Under overload the buffer keeps younger updates, so fresh changes infect a few members first and the rest once the rate quiets.
Partitions only delay: challenge 3c passes when every value reaches every node by the end of the run, because re-contact after healing carries the backlog.
Convergence is the whole contract. Gossip promises nothing about recency, order or durability, so a converged read can still be stale.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, run the rumor model: with \(n = 100\) and fanout 1 the rounds give 2, 4, 8 and 16, and full cover needs 7 rounds since \(2^7 = 128\). With \(n = 10\) and fanout 2 the third round computes 27 and caps at 10.
traps: Quoting the doubling curve as measured behavior. Duplicate contacts and slow nodes stretch every round, so treat the model as the ceiling and your run as the floor.
Reading convergence as consistency. Two nodes can converge on different values at different times with no violation; ordering needs the clocks from earlier units.
Gossiping full state every round. The 3b page calls that impractical; send deltas or digests, and keep per-round bytes bounded as the cluster grows.

selfTest.q: Fanout 2, ten nodes, one informed. How many rounds to cover all, and what caps the math?
selfTest.a: Three: 3, 9, then 27 capped at 10. The cap is the cluster size; extra contacts after cover are duplicates.

selfTest.q: Why does SWIM prefer younger buffer entries when piggyback space runs out?
selfTest.a: Fresh changes must infect someone quickly or they stall everywhere. Once the injection rate quiets, the backlog still propagates through later rounds.

selfTest.q: A 3c run converges but one read missed a late write. Bug or expected?
selfTest.a: Expected. The checker tests convergence by end of run, not recency, so a read may miss a write that had not arrived yet.

selfTest.q: Your 5-node run converges in 2 seconds. Does gossip guarantee 2-second convergence at 50 nodes?
selfTest.a: No. Rounds grow slowly but per-round work, duplicates and the partition schedule all change; remeasure on the new setup.

practice.name: Gossip Glomers 3a to 3c: Broadcast
practice.locator: Run 3a with `--node-count 1 --time-limit 20 --rate 10`, 3b with `--node-count 5`, and 3c adding `--nemesis partition`, each with `--bin` pointing at your binary; keep every run directory
practice.note: Read messages-per-operation and stable latencies from your own 3c results file as a labeled example, and compare convergence rounds with the rumor model.

practice.name: Simulate Gossip Rumor Spread
practice.locator: Implement `spread` with `informed = min(n, informed * (1 + fanout))` per round, capping late rounds at `n`; the examples cover doubling and the 27-to-10 cap
practice.note: Do this before the cluster runs. It fixes the ceiling your measured spread must sit under.

units.stopWhen: The rumor examples pass from memory, 3c passes with its run directory kept, and you can explain your measured rounds as model ceiling plus duplicates.

fit.note: SWIM plus the required Glomers chain cover dissemination and measurement, with the free rumor drill as the model check.

units.title: Membership join, leave and replacement, versioned views and stale-view handling
outcomes: Run join, leave, suspect, alive and failed transitions and say which message overrides which.
Version membership views and reject stale ones on receipt and before acting.
Handle replacement: a restarted member rejoins without its old identity hijacking the view.
units.why: A membership list is a replicated object with stale readers. Versioning is what stops a healed partition from resurrecting the dead.

next.note: Decide which side of a partition may change the view.
Replay join, leave and replacement under seeded faults.

study.title: Join, leave and refutation
study.locator: Section 3.2 (join through a contact member or coordinator, leave by announcement) with Section 4.1 (buffered dissemination) and Section 4.2 (Suspect refuted by Alive with a higher incarnation, Failed after the timeout)

study.title: The majority rules on death declarations
study.locator: Chapter 9, The Majority Rules (pp. 372-373): the one-way-listening node, the minute-long pause, and why a quorum must declare death

focus: Join needs a contact: a coordinator, a well-known address, or probabilistic replies. Leave is an announcement over unreliable spread, so treat it as a hint and keep probing.
Suspect is not Failed. A suspected member stays on the list and stays a probe target until the timeout passes with no Alive refutation.
Higher incarnation wins for one member's reports. Alive at 4 refutes Suspect at 3, and a late Failed at 3 is dropped, not applied.
Death declarations belong to a quorum, not to one watcher. A node that hears only itself, like the book's one-way listener, must step down when the majority disagrees.
Replacement is a new epoch, never a reset counter. The group still holds the old incarnation, so a restart that reuses it splits the view.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, apply this sequence for member A: Suspect at incarnation 3, Alive at incarnation 4, then a delayed Failed at incarnation 3. Final view: A alive at 4, with the Failed dropped as stale. State the comparison each message needs: member id, then incarnation, then type precedence.
traps: Deleting a failed member immediately. Late refutations and delayed messages then have nowhere to land; keep the recently failed alongside the living, as SWIM does.
Acting on one reporter's Failed. A partition makes every watcher on one side wrong together; wait for quorum agreement before reassigning work.
Trusting leave as certain. A lost leave leaves a ghost member, and a lost join leaves a live stranger; both need the probe path as backup.

selfTest.q: Two watchers report Failed for A at incarnation 3 while A broadcasts Alive at 4. What is A's state?
selfTest.a: Alive at 4. Reports compare by incarnation first, and 4 beats any number of 3s regardless of reporter count.

selfTest.q: A node restarts and rejoins with incarnation 0 while the group holds it failed at incarnation 2. What happens without an epoch?
selfTest.a: Its reports lose every comparison, and its old identity shadows the new one. It must rejoin under a fresh epoch the group has never seen.

selfTest.q: Why does the book make the one-way-listening node step down instead of defending itself?
selfTest.a: It cannot prove its case to anyone: its outgoing path is dead. Only a quorum decision both sides can observe breaks the symmetry.

selfTest.q: A leave announcement never arrives. How does the group still converge?
selfTest.a: Probes keep failing, suspicion rises through the normal path, and the member is declared failed by timeout rather than by announcement.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: versioned membership views with join, leave and replacement, plus stale-view tests where delayed Suspect, Alive and Failed messages arrive out of order with seeds retained.
units.stopWhen: You apply the reproduce sequence with the drop reason stated per message, and can argue any override dispute from incarnation numbers alone.

fit.note: SWIM plus DDIA cover transitions and quorum death at explain and implement depth, with view practice assigned to the section mini-project.

units.title: Partitions, asymmetric reachability, split-brain boundaries and correlated failure domains
outcomes: Draw two-sided and one-sided partitions with asymmetric reachability, and say what each node may conclude.
State the split-brain boundary: which side may act under a majority rule, and what the minority must do.
Map nodes to failure domains and give one correlated fault that a per-node model misses.
units.why: A partition turns one cluster into two truths. This unit draws the line the minority must not cross, and names the shared fate that per-node thinking misses.

next.note: Enforce the minority-stop rule with fencing when clocks and pauses conspire.
See how consensus keeps one truth across the same partitions.

study.title: Knowledge, majorities and system models
study.locator: Chapter 9, Knowledge, Truth, and Lies (pp. 371-372): guesses from messages and stating the model; The Majority Rules (pp. 372-373): quorum death declarations; System Model and Reality (pp. 380-384): synchronous, partially synchronous and asynchronous timing with crash-stop, crash-recovery, limping and Byzantine nodes

study.title: Partition behavior on a real run
study.locator: Challenge 3c: five nodes with `--nemesis partition`; watch which nodes the checker still converges and which values wait for healing
study.depth: Read the run as a partition log, not only a pass. Note what no node could conclude mid-run about the other side.

focus: A partition is not death: both sides keep running with different knowledge. One-sided reachability is worse, since the cut-off node hears requests it can never answer.
Under a majority rule of more than half, only a side holding the majority may decide. With five nodes split 3 and 2, the 2 must stop deciding, even while fully healthy.
The book's model advice: design for partial synchrony with crash recovery, where delays, pauses and drift are usually bounded but sometimes arbitrarily large. Safety must survive the sometimes.

Failure domains are shared fate: one rack, switch, power feed or zone holds many nodes. The Systems unit on failure domains, correctness signals and safe rollout maps the practice; here learn the correlated cases it assumes, like a deploy or a config pushed everywhere at once.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, apply the majority rule to five nodes: split 3 and 2 means only the 3 acts; after one more failure leaves 2 and 2, neither side holds 3, so both stop. State the general rule: with \(2f + 1\) nodes, progress needs \(f + 1\) on one side.
traps: Letting both sides serve writes and merge later without a plan. Without CRDTs or a stated conflict rule that is split brain with a nicer name.
Treating one peer's heartbeat as cluster connectivity. Reachability is pairwise and asymmetric; a green link to one node says nothing about the rest.
Counting live nodes instead of a fixed membership. A majority is out of all members, not out of the currently reachable ones, or two sides each claim it.

selfTest.q: Node A hears B, B does not hear A, and both hear C. What can A conclude about B?
selfTest.a: Only that its own messages to B go unanswered. B may be dead, partitioned one way, or merely slow; A must not declare B dead alone.

selfTest.q: Seven nodes split 4 and 3. Which side decides, and what must the 3 do?
selfTest.a: The 4 decides, holding more than half of 7. The 3 serves nothing that needs agreement and waits for healing or reassignment.

selfTest.q: A rolling config push restarts every node within a minute. Per-node thinking says fine. What is wrong?
selfTest.a: The restarts correlate: the fault shares one cause and one window. The cluster can lose majority together, which independent-failure math never predicts.

selfTest.q: Why does the book call partial synchrony with crash recovery the most useful model?
selfTest.a: It matches reality: timing usually holds but sometimes breaks without bound, and crashed nodes return with stable storage intact. Safety must hold in the bad intervals; only progress may wait them out.

practice.name: Building Distributed Systems Timekeeper PH-3: Simulate Split-Brain Caused by Clock Drift
practice.locator: Task PH-3: drive two sides of a partition to claim one lease through skewed clocks
practice.note: Keep the losing side's log: the observable you want is both sides believing they hold it, which fencing must later refuse.

units.stopWhen: You apply the majority rule to any split without notes, and your PH-3 log shows the double-claim your fencing design must refuse.

fit.note: DDIA plus the partition run cover boundaries and domains at explain depth, with the free split-brain drill as checked practice.

units.title: Leases, process pauses, fencing tokens and a lease implementation
outcomes: State the lease contract and the three timing assumptions it stands on.
Construct a pause scenario that lets an expired holder write, and show fencing blocking it.
Implement lease acquire, renew and release with monotonic fencing tokens, tested for expiry, pause and partition cases.
units.why: A lease is authority with an expiry date. Pauses forge the date, so the storage layer must check the token, not the clock.

next.note: Fence stale leaders the same way after partitions.
Replay pause and partition schedules against your lease.

study.title: Pauses, leases and fencing
study.locator: Chapter 9, Process Pauses (pp. 366-371): the lease-renewal loop with its two flaws and the pause catalog; Distributed Locks and Leases (pp. 373-377): the HBase zombie, fencing tokens 33 and 34 with Figure 9-6, and fencing across replicas with Figure 9-7

study.title: Fencing tokens and the pause race
study.locator: Making the lock safe with fencing (tokens 33 and 34 with storage-side rejection); the check-then-write pause race; the Redlock synchrony assumptions
study.depth: Treat the Redlock critique as dated to 2016. The lasting lesson is the token rule, not the product verdict.

focus: A lease says the holder may act until expiry and the granter may reassign after. It assumes bounded clock error for comparing expiry, bounded pauses between check and act, and timely renewal delivery. Break any one and authority overlaps.
The book's loop fails twice: expiry set by one machine is read against another's clock, and a 15-second pause between the validity check and the request lets the lease die mid-act unnoticed.

Fencing moves enforcement to storage: every grant carries a higher token, here 33 then 34, and storage rejects any write whose token moved backward. The lock service grants; the storage service refuses.
Token sources must already be monotonic per resource: Chubby sequencers, Kafka epochs, ZooKeeper version numbers, etcd revisions. A token that resets on failover reopens the hole.

With replicas, put the token in the most significant bits of the timestamp and write a quorum. A zombie write can still land on one missed replica, but the next quorum read prefers the higher token and repair overwrites it.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, walk tokens 33 and 34: client 1 holds 33 and pauses past expiry; client 2 takes 34 and writes; client 1 resumes and writes with 33, which storage rejects as backward. State the storage invariant: the largest token seen wins, and anything lower is refused.
traps: Renewing early and then pausing. The renewal only proves liveness at renewal time; a pause after it still expires the lease under the holder.
Releasing or renewing without matching owner and token. Any holder that can release another's lease can steal authority without waiting.
Generating tokens from a counter that resets on lock-service failover. Tokens must be monotonic across crashes too, or the new service reissues 33 after 34.

selfTest.q: Why must the fencing check live on the storage service rather than the lock service?
selfTest.a: The paused holder never contacts the lock service again; it goes straight to storage believing its lease is live. Only storage sees the stale write and can refuse it.

selfTest.q: Client 1 holds token 33 with 30 seconds left, then pauses 60 seconds. Client 2 holds 34 and writes twice. Client 1 resumes and writes. Which writes survive?
selfTest.a: Client 2's two writes survive. Client 1's write carries 33 against a seen 34 and is rejected, even though 33 was valid when issued.

selfTest.q: The lock service crashes and restarts, reissuing token 33 to a new holder while 34 exists. What breaks?
selfTest.a: Monotonicity breaks: storage has seen 34, so it rejects the legitimate new holder's 33. Token state needs the same durability as the lease.

selfTest.q: Client 2 reaches only two of three replicas with token 34. Where can client 1's token-33 write still land, and why is that safe?
selfTest.a: On the missed third replica. It stays safe because reads go to a quorum, which always includes a replica holding 34, and repair then overwrites the stale copy.

practice.name: Implement a Lease Lock with Fencing Tokens
practice.locator: Implement `acquire`, `renew` and `release`: a lease at `now` expires at `now + ttl` and is active while `now < expiresAt`, tokens rise by one per grant and are never reused; the examples map Alice and Bob through expiry at time 10 and release at time 8
practice.note: After it passes, add the storage-side token check the page omits: a write with a backward token must be rejected even from the recorded holder.

units.stopWhen: You walk the 33 and 34 case with the invariant stated, and your lock passes the problem's expiry examples plus your own pause-and-stale-write test.

fit.note: DDIA plus the locking essay cover pauses and fencing but give no checked practice; the owned AlgoMaster lease drill supplies it.

units.title: Deterministic membership and network simulation
outcomes: Build a seeded scheduler with delay, drop, duplicate, reorder, partition and crash faults that replays byte-identical traces.
Run membership, detector and lease logic inside it against the DS-2 fault slice of the project list.
Reduce a failing run to a seed plus schedule and retain it as evidence.
units.why: Simulation is how one machine tests a cluster. Determinism turns a flaky failure into a reproducible case the learner can argue from.

next.note: Reuse the harness for replication faults and repair.
Drive the same schedules from property tests.

study.title: Deterministic faults and durable histories
study.locator: Architecture constraints (deterministic schedules, durable event histories, timing-free safety tests) with the failure-injection list entries for this section: split brain attempt, clock jump, stale lease and epoch, and dual process incarnation
study.depth: Read the DS-2 slice only. The log, stream and transaction entries belong to later sections.

study.title: An external behavior contract
study.locator: Challenge 3c evaluation: every broadcast value visible on every node after a partitioned run
study.depth: Use as the conformance target your simulated broadcast must also satisfy. The Systems unit on distributed histories and deterministic failure simulation built the scheduler itself; extend it here, do not rebuild it.

focus: Seed everything: topology, delays, drops, duplicates, reorder windows, partition intervals, crash and restart points. A run is its seed plus its schedule, and both are retained.
Simulate time as an integer tick, never the wall clock. Timers, heartbeats and lease checks read the tick, so reruns cannot drift.
Safety checks must not read timing: membership convergence, suspicion traces and fencing verdicts are functions of delivered messages and ticks only. Name liveness assumptions separately.
Cover the DS-2 slice: split brain attempt, clock jump, stale lease and epoch, dual incarnation, pause and partition healing. Later sections add their own entries to the same harness.
Keep raw message and state traces, then minimize: shrink the schedule to the smallest seed that still fails before reporting.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, state the determinism contract: same seed plus same schedule gives byte-identical message and state traces on rerun. Demonstrate it by running a three-node partition schedule twice and diffing the two trace files, which must match exactly.
traps: Seeding the network but reading the wall clock in a timeout. One unseeded time source makes reruns diverge and the diff lie.
Testing only loss-free schedules. Discovery lives in drops, duplicates, reorder and pause interleavings; the clean run is the smoke test, not the evidence.
Keeping summaries instead of raw traces. A minimized case needs the full message history, or the next reader cannot replay the verdict.

selfTest.q: Two reruns of one seed disagree. Name three unseeded sources that could explain it.
selfTest.a: Wall-clock reads, an unseeded RNG such as a default hash seed or thread race, and iteration over an unordered set or map. Fix all three before trusting any diff.

selfTest.q: Why must safety checks avoid the tick, not just the wall clock?
selfTest.a: A check that reads simulated time can pass at one tick and fail at another for the same messages. Safety must follow from message content and order alone.

selfTest.q: A dual-incarnation bug appears once in fifty seeds. What do you keep?
selfTest.a: The failing seed, the schedule, the raw trace, and the minimized variant. The other forty-nine runs are the coverage note, not the evidence.

selfTest.q: Your simulated broadcast converges under every partition schedule. Does 3c still add anything?
selfTest.a: Yes, as an independent oracle: it runs your real node binary over a real network stack, catching harness blind spots like framing or protocol bugs the sim cannot see.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: the deterministic membership and network simulation harness with seeded schedules, retained raw traces and one minimized failure case.
units.stopWhen: Your rerun diff is empty, the DS-2 fault slice all runs inside the harness, and one minimized case is retained with its seed.

fit.note: Project contract plus the Glomers oracle cover the simulation slice at implement depth, extending the Systems scheduler unit with mini-project practice.
